opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason is that I believe the most important thing for making AI go well is having safety-focused people at the frontier, actually building the most capable systems. A lot of the safety problems we care about only really show up, or only become tractable to study, once you have models that are close to the cutting edge. If you're working on alignment with models that are a couple of generations behind, you're always guessing about what the real problems will look like. At Anthropic we get to work directly with frontier models, see how they actually behave, find where things break, and test whether our techniques hold up as models scale.

The second piece is influence. If a lab that takes safety seriously is also competitive, it can shape norms across the industry. Things like the Responsible Scaling Policy were meant to show that you can commit ahead of time to specific safety measures tied to capability levels, and ideally other labs adopt similar commitments, and eventually that informs regulation. You can only really set that example credibly if you're actually at the frontier. If you're far behind, nobody cares what your safety policy says.

And then there's the culture internally. Safety isn't a side team that people tolerate. It's woven into how decisions get made. Leadership started the company specifically because they were worried about this, and that shows up in things like how we decide what to release, how much we invest in interpretability and alignment research, and the fact that people across the org, including on the training side where I work, think about risks as part of their day-to-day job.

I should be honest that there's a real tension here. Building frontier models means you're contributing to the pace of AI progress, and I take that seriously. It's not obvious this is the right bet. But when I weigh it up, I'd rather there be a lab at the frontier that's deeply focused on getting this right than leave the frontier entirely to organizations that care less. That's the bet, and so far I think it's been a reasonable one, though it's something I keep reevaluating.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the key to making AI go well is having safety-focused people build frontier systems, and describes safety as shared across the organization and embedded in decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is: I think powerful AI is coming, probably sooner than most people expect, and I don't think the question is really whether it gets built. The question is who builds it and how carefully. And given that, I think it's really valuable to have labs at the frontier that are genuinely focused on safety, that take the risks seriously, and that have the capability to actually do the research on the most capable models.

Anthropic was founded pretty explicitly around that premise. The idea was something like: if you believe this technology is going to be transformative and potentially dangerous, you want to be in a position where you can actually influence how it goes. And a lot of the most important safety work, things like interpretability, alignment research, red-teaming, evaluations of dangerous capabilities, you really need access to frontier models to do well. You can't study the failure modes of a model that doesn't exist yet or that you don't have access to.

So one piece of it is that we're at the frontier, and that lets the safety research be grounded in what's actually happening rather than what we imagine might happen.

The other piece is about the broader ecosystem. I think having a safety-focused lab at the frontier shifts things for everyone. It raises the bar on what responsible development looks like. Things like the Responsible Scaling Policy, where we commit to specific safety measures before we scale to certain capability levels, that's the kind of thing where, if it works, other labs feel pressure to adopt something similar. And it gives policymakers concrete examples of what's possible, rather than just abstract proposals.

I'd also say, on a more personal level, I work on pretraining, which is a very capabilities-focused role. And I think people sometimes find that surprising, like, why would someone who cares about safety work on making the models more capable? My view is that the models are going to get more capable regardless, and I'd rather that happen somewhere with the culture and the institutional commitments to do it carefully. And honestly, a lot of the safety-relevant work happens in the details of how you train the model, what you train it on, how you think about the tradeoffs. Having people who care about the outcome in those seats matters.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. There's a real tension in being a company that's building the thing you're worried about. I think that tension is something we have to take seriously and keep examining. But on balance, I think it's the right bet, and I think it's one of the better places to be if you want to actually move the needle on this.

r001.rationale: The response says safety-focused frontier labs and having people who care in key roles can help make AI go well, but it does not argue that assembling a collectively focused team is the best way to achieve that outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic case is that if you want to make advanced AI go well, it helps to be somewhere you can both understand the systems and influence how they’re developed. Working at a frontier lab gives you access to the models, the infrastructure, and the people making those decisions. You can test safety ideas against the systems they actually need to work on, and feed what you learn back into training and deployment.

The other part is whether the organization takes those questions seriously. What makes Anthropic promising to me is the ambition to put safety at the center of that work, alongside the technical capability to make progress on it.

That’s not a guarantee that everything we do is right, or that working at a frontier lab is the best choice for everyone. There’s a real tension between developing more capable systems and managing the risks they create. But I think having people who care deeply about those risks in a position to do concrete research and affect decisions is valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says it is valuable for people who care about AI risks to do research and influence decisions, but it does not argue that assembling a collectively focused team is the best way to make AI go well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic case is that if you want to make AI go well, it’s really valuable to have safety research closely connected to the systems that are actually being built. You can have ideas about what might go wrong, test those ideas on capable models, and then use what you learn to change how the next model is trained or deployed.

One thing I find promising about Anthropic is that there are people across the organisation who take the risks seriously. That matters because safety isn’t just a research problem. It also involves decisions about what to build, how to evaluate it, and when you have enough confidence to release it.

I wouldn’t say that makes success guaranteed. There are real tensions involved in building powerful AI while trying to understand and reduce its risks. But it seems like a place where you can work directly on those problems, with access to the models and the people making consequential decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic has people across the organisation who take AI risks seriously, but it does not argue that assembling a collectively focused team is the best way to make AI go well.
